text: The Woman Who Records the Wind
Last spring I read an article about a woman who lives alone at the edge of the desert.
She used to work in an office downtown, but she could not live that way any longer.
Now she gets up before dawn to record the wind.
Her house is close to a dry riverbed, and the wind there can tear a door off its hinges.
On the morning I visited, a single tear ran down her cheek as she watched a storm close in.
"I wound the rope around the post," she said, holding up her hand, "and then I noticed the wound."
Her neighbour plays bass in a country band, and on weekends the two of them fish for bass in the reservoir.
Last year his band set a record for the longest live show in the county.
He had to bow so many times that he joked about tying a bow around his neck and calling it a night.
Her project is simple.
She wants to present the sounds of the place exactly as they are.
"I object to the idea that silence is empty," she told me.
"The content of one quiet minute is enormous.
Even minute changes in the air tell you a story."
She keeps her chairs in a row on the porch, although she and her brother once had a row about who would inherit them.
Her grandmother was Polish, and the old silver still gets a polish every winter.
The farm does produce a few vegetables, and she sells the produce at the market in town.
She needed a permit to work in the national park, and the rangers would only permit it at night.
She hopes to resume that work in the fall, and she showed me a resume that listed every park she has recorded in.
She lives a modest life, and she is content.
Her refuse goes to a heap behind the barn, and she would refuse any offer to sell the land.
Every few months she has to separate the good takes from the bad and keep them in a separate folder.
She guesses she has two thousand hours of tape, although she admits that this is a rough estimate.
When I asked whether the work had changed her, she was quiet for a minute.
"I learned to listen," she said.
"Not like a learned professor.
More like that dove on the roof.
Yesterday a hawk dove at it, and it didn't even flinch."
Before I left, she asked me to read her guest book.
I read it on the train home, and I have read it twice since.
There is no use pretending I was not moved.
I used the quiet carriage to write this, and I will use it again on the way back.
The storms there have changed a lot of lives, but I don't think she would ever desert that place.
Her old pipes were made of lead, so this summer she will lead a small crew to replace them.
In April she will sow beans, and the old sow next door will try to dig them up.
Nobody there seems upset about it.
